summary.text: Laplace expansion is one way to view and compute a determinant, and it is valued for its simplicity.
It is often useful in proofs because it allows recursion on the size of matrices.
For large matrices it quickly becomes inefficient compared with Gaussian elimination.

facts.label: Main strength
facts.value: Simple, and often useful in proofs

facts.label: Also called
facts.value: Cofactor expansion, named after Pierre-Simon Laplace

items.prompt: A program must find the determinant of a very large matrix. Which method will serve it better than Laplace expansion?

options.label: Repeating Laplace expansion on every entry
Guessing from the first row alone
Expanding along columns instead of rows
Gaussian elimination

items.explain: For large matrices, Laplace expansion quickly becomes inefficient compared with Gaussian elimination.

items.prompt: A mathematician wants to prove something about determinants of every size by building up from smaller matrices. Why is Laplace expansion handy?

options.label: It allows recursion on the size of matrices
It is the fastest method for large matrices
It avoids ever using smaller matrices
It only works for the smallest matrices

items.explain: The expansion is often useful in proofs because it allows recursion on the size of matrices.

items.prompt: In a square matrix, adding the first column to the third column gives exactly double the second column. What can be said about its determinant?

options.label: It must be one
It must be zero
It must be negative
It cannot be known

items.explain: That relation among the columns makes the matrix singular, so its determinant is zero.

items.prompt: A student uses Laplace expansion on a 4 by 4 matrix. What does the method turn the determinant into?

options.label: A single product of all sixteen entries
The plain sum of all sixteen entries
The largest entry of the matrix
A sum of terms built from 3 by 3 determinants

items.explain: The expansion writes the determinant of an n × n matrix as a weighted sum of minors, which are determinants of (n − 1) × (n − 1) submatrices.

items.prompt: A matrix has columns where the first plus the third equals twice the second, and its determinant is zero. What label fits such a matrix?

options.label: Invertible
Orthogonal
Singular
Triangular

items.explain: The matrix is described as singular because of that column relation, and its determinant is zero.

items.prompt: A friend says Laplace expansion is pointless because it is slow for big matrices. What is a fair reply?

options.label: Agreed, it has no use at all
It is simple and useful in proofs, even if slow
It is actually faster than Gaussian elimination
It only gives wrong answers for big matrices

items.explain: It is slow for large matrices, but it is simple, often useful in proofs, and one of several ways to view the determinant.
